title: Workshop on Carbohydrate Moieties as Vaccine Candidates
abstract: Workshop on Carbohydrate Moieties as Vaccine Candidates Bethesda, MD, USA October 6-7, 2004 Whole microbes, microbial subunits and extracts, and peptide and protein antigens have been the focus of much vaccine research and development. While studies of peptide and protein antigens have been facilitated by the rapid advances in genomics and proteomics, studies of sugar chains, which are abundantly expressed on the outer surfaces of viral, bacterial, protozoan, and fungal pathogens and on the membranes of mammalian cells, have not kept pace with technologic advances. Polysaccharide-based vaccines have demonstrated efficacy in disease-prevention strategies, e.g., Haemophilus influenzae b and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines. However, our understanding of several aspects of polysaccharide vaccines is limited, and more knowledge is needed to allow greater development and deployment. The goals of this workshop were to examine the mechanisms involved in generating an appropriate immune response to selected carbohydrate antigens, highlight recent and novel advances, and discuss how this information could be used in the development of effective vaccines. The workshop participants included national and international research scientists and clinicians from the National Institutes of Health, the Food and Drug Administration, academia, and industry. The meeting was organized into 7 sessions on such topics as genetic and cellular mechanisms of carbohydrate immunity, carbohydrate antigens for vaccines, and new tools for studying carbohydrates. Understanding the mechanistic aspects of the genetic control and the cellular pathways of the immune response to bacterial carbohydrate antigens should provide insights into ways to enhance the immune response and thus facilitate vaccine development. Studies were also presented on novel molecules involved in the recognition of carbohydrate antigens such as specific intercellular adhesion molecule (ICAM)–grabbing nonintegrins, which are C-type lectins that show substantial expression in many tissues, and toll-like receptors, which function as pattern recognition receptors for conserved pathogen structures and serve as key links between innate and adaptive immunity. Investigations are ongoing to determine how these molecules function in bacterial clearance and in signaling innate and adaptive responses. A number of presentations were focused on the role of CD1 proteins, which present lipid antigens (e.g., from mycobacteria or Francisella tularensis, a potential weapon of bioterrorism) to T cells. The evidence that CD1-restricted T cells contribute to immunity against microbial infection includes the observation that CD1 is expressed at higher levels in lesions of tuberculoid leprosy in comparison to lepromatous leprosy. The design of optimal vaccines against such pathogens should include lipid and peptide antigens. Presentations from several invited experts emphasized the current challenges facing the development of vaccines for meningococcal meningitis. Given that group B meningococcal capsular polysaccharide is similar to host molecules, studies are ongoing to identify vaccine candidates that elicit protective antibody without eliciting autoantibodies. A licensed outer membrane vesicle vaccine was recently introduced for widespread use in New Zealand to control an epidemic. Regarding groups A and C polysaccharides, differences exist in age-related immune responses; for example, for unknown reasons group A polysaccharide is uniquely immunogenic in infants as young as 6 months of age and repeated doses elicit booster antibody responses, whereas group C is poorly immunogenic and repeated doses do not induce adequate responses. A continuing problem in vaccine research is devising methods to enhance the immune response and then ensuring that it is protective against disease; for instance, the use of CD40 agonist antibody plus antigen showed remarkably rapid immune response and protection in a murine model of anthrax. Equally challenging are efforts to develop combined and multivalent vaccines; several new approaches were discussed. For instance, a diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B, H. influenzae b, meningococcal A and C combination vaccine has been tested in an open, randomized, controlled study. It induces groups A and C bactericidal antibody responses in infants and has reactogenicity profiles similar to meningococcal A and C conjugates given separately. Recent efforts in HIV vaccine research indicate that producing a multivalent envelope glycan conjugate vaccine to induce production of broad neutralizing antibodies is possible. New technologies such as carbohydrate microarrays, automated syntheses of oligosaccharides, and biophysical and computational methods for studying antigen-antibody interactions are now available for providing insight into the structure of and immune response to carbohydrate antigens. Additionally, peptide mimotopes may be used in carbohydrate technologies designed for proteins. An oligosaccharide synthesizer is now being used in the development of a number of vaccines, including those for malaria, leishmaniasis, HIV, tuberculosis, and leprosy. A Consortium for Functional Genomics (Web site available from http://www.functionalglycomics.org) has been established at the Scripps Research Institute and has developed a novel glycan array format that uses covalent coupling of glycans to glass slides. At the conclusion of the workshop, participants were asked to identify gaps in knowledge and resource needs. The gaps include 1) elucidating the mechanisms of immunity to and regulation of carbohydrate antigens in adults, children, and neonates and using opportunities (e.g., computer capacity) for modeling carbohydrate antigen-antibody interactions; 2) defining the molecular basis of enhanced immunogenicity with glycoconjugate vaccines and investigating the role of adjuvants; 3) examining the role of CD1-reactive T cells in the immune response to capsular polysaccharides; and 4) developing surrogates for in vivo immunity for the use of glycolipids as CD1-based vaccines in humans. Resource needs include the following: 1) enhanced availability of carbohydrate microarrays; 2) development of appropriate animal models and the availability of a transgenic mouse platform that allows generation of human antibodies; 3) development of tetramers and analytical chemistry to help in the identification of antigens, e.g., for the use of glycolipids as CD-1-based vaccines; and 4) enhanced good laboratory practice (GLP) resources to produce synthetic carbohydrate vaccines and GLP testing for vaccine candidate safety in animals and for production of good manufacturing practice vaccine candidates. As a result of the workshop, an open LISTSERV (GLYCOIMMUNOLOGY) has been established, and the Journal of Clinical Infectious Diseases will publish a review article. For additional information, contact ctaylor@niaid.nih.gov The workshop was sponsored by funds from the National Vaccine Program Office and the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

title: Brain endothelial cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway in aging and neurodegeneration
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway has emerged as a key mediator of neuroinflammation. While current studies primarily attribute its effects to neurons and glial cells, emerging research suggests that cGAS-STING signaling may play a critical role in cerebral vasculature, particularly in brain endothelial cells. Therefore, studying the role of inflammation caused by the cGAS–STING pathway in brain endothelial cells could provide a more comprehensive understanding of neuroinflammatory disease and new avenues for therapeutic interventions. Here, we review the multifaceted role of global cGAS–STING signaling in various neurological and neuroinflammatory diseases and the potential contribution of cGAS–STING in brain endothelial cells. The vascular system in the brain creates a unique environment crucial for proper brain functioning (Sweeney et al., 2019). Inflammation in blood vessels compromises both vascular and cerebral function. It is increasingly recognized as a critical factor contributing to the development of various neurological disorders. Recent research has indicated that cGAS–STING signaling, an innate immunity pathway (Paul et al., 2021), may play a central role in vascular inflammation. Neurovascular inflammation in aging and neurodegeneration: Neuroinflammation is a prevalent feature and plays a pivotal role in aging and neurodegenerative disorders (Paul et al., 2021). While neuroglia are increasingly studied in aging and neurodegeneration, less is known about the contribution of the vasculature and brain endothelial cells (BECs), which represent another significant site of inflammation in the central nervous system (CNS). Neurovascular inflammation results in blood–brain barrier (BBB) leakage, dysfunction of the neurovascular unit, and hypoxia. This amplifies the inflammatory response within the CNS, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and damage (Sweeney et al., 2019). As the primary barrier in blood vessels between blood and the surrounding tissues, the endothelial cells (ECs) are a key player in vascular inflammation. BECs have especially great importance as they—together with pericytes and astrocytes—form the multicellular BBB and contribute to the selective permeability of the BBB (Sweeney et al., 2019). By interacting with both immune signaling molecules in the blood and CNS immune cells, BECs act as an important bridge between functions of the innate immune system, making them an interesting target for anti-inflammatory treatment. Endothelial inflammation is a multifaceted process involving various mechanisms. Recent research has indicated that the cGAS-STING pathway may be involved in triggering the inflammatory processes in endothelial cells (Yu et al., 2022). The aim of this perspective is to examine the potential role of BEC cGAS–STING in various neurological and neuroinflammatory diseases. We first review the role of global cGAS–STING signaling in these diseases. We then discuss the current evidence of the cGAS–STING pathway in triggering endothelial inflammation and dysfunction. The cGas–STING pathway overview: cGAS–STING signaling serves as a crucial regulator of inflammatory responses (Paul et al., 2021). This pathway, designed to sense DNA within the cell and trigger an immune response, acts as a surveillance mechanism for damaged and infected cells. DNA triggering this response can originate from diverse sources. Pathogenic sources include double-stranded DNA viruses, retroviruses, some intracellular bacteria, and parasitic protozoans. Moreover, self-DNA—both extracellular and genomic—and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can also activate cGAS under specific circumstances (Paul et al., 2021). cGAS recognizes long double-stranded DNA in the cytoplasm and undergoes activation to synthesize 2′,3′-cGAMP (Figure 1). This molecule then binds to STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, leading to STING oligomerization and translocation to the Golgi. In the Golgi, STING recruits TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) to form a signalosome, facilitating TBK1 autophosphorylation. Subsequently, TBK1 phosphorylates STING, providing a docking site for interferon (IFN) regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), which is also phosphorylated by TBK1. Activated IRF3 forms dimers and translocates to the nucleus, stimulating the transcription of type I IFNs and other IFN-stimulated genes. Additionally, the cGAS-STING pathway activates nuclear factor-κB, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and the STING-PERK signalosome within the endoplasmic reticulum, further contributing to the ensuing immune response.Figure 1: Schematic diagram of activation of the cGAS–STING signaling pathway in BECs.During aging and neurogenerative conditions, cytosolic DNA is recognized by cGAS, leading to the synthesis of a 2′,3′-cGAMP. 2′,3′-cGAMP binds to STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, causing STING transportation to the proximity of the Golgi, where it recruits TBK-1. TBK1 phosphorylates STING, activating the transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB. Activated IRF3 and NF-κB then travel to the nucleus to promote the transcription of type I IFNs and NF-κB inflammatory genes. Alternatively, the cGAS-STING pathway can be activated independently of the DNA sensing pathway. Excessive and continuous production and release of IFN and other inflammatory cytokines resulting from activation of the cGAS-STING pathway can lead to BEC inflammation and dysfunction. This dysfunction results in BBB leakage, allowing IFN, other inflammatory cytokines, plasma proteins, and blood immune cells to permeate into the brain parenchyma. Ultimately, this contributes to the escalation of the neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative process. Created with BioRender.com. BBB: Blood–brain barrier; BEC: brain endothelial cell; cGAS: cyclic GMP–AMP synthase; dsDNA: double-stranded DNA; EC: endothelial cell; IFN: interferon; IRF3: interferon regulatory factor 3; mtDNA: mitochondrial DNA; NF-κB: nuclear factor kappa B; STING: stimulator of interferon genes; TBK1: TANK-binding kinase 1.While the cGAS–STING pathway plays a prominent role in anti-viral, anti-tumor, and inflammatory responses through driving IFN and cytokine production, cGAS and STING also have various functions outside of immunity. cGAS–STING signaling in aging and neurodegeneration: Neuroinflammation emerges as a significant hallmark in numerous neurological disorders. Given the pivotal role of the cGAS–STING pathway in inflammatory processes, there is a compelling rationale to thoroughly investigate this pathway in the context of neurological disorders (Paul et al., 2021). Notably, the cGAS–STING pathway has been implicated in diverse neurological conditions such as brain injury, aging, and neurodegenerative disorders. In particular, brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are highlighted in the following discussion. Aging is the predominant risk factor for the majority of neurodegenerative diseases, often accompanied by the accumulation of senescent cells and inflammation, commonly referred to as inflammaging (Paul et al., 2021). Senescent cells exhibit significant secretory activity known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. The dysregulated activity of cGAS–STING is consistently observed among various types of senescent cells, playing a crucial role in the secretion of several senescence-associated secretory phenotype components. Mechanistically, the cGAS–STING pathway triggers the senescence-associated secretory phenotype secretion through the accumulation of cytoplasmic DNA, which is released into the cytosol from the nucleus and mitochondria in senescent cells (Paul et al., 2021). Research has demonstrated that aging-related inflammation is driven by cGAS–STING activation (Gulen et al., 2023). Notably, inhibiting the cGAS-STING pathway in aged mice has been shown to prevent aging-related inflammation and enhance cognitive and motor performance (Gulen et al., 2023). Upon reflection of these findings, it is possible to speculate that the aberrant signaling of cGAS–STING contributes to age-related dysfunction through its pro-inflammatory properties. AD is the most common neurodegenerative disease. Within AD, the aggregation of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau induces cellular stress, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction and the release of mtDNA, which is subsequently recognized by cGAS (Xie et al., 2023). This process triggers heightened expression of type I IFN, provoking neuroinflammation characterized by astrogliosis and microglial activation. Notably, in AD, the STING–IRF3 pathway seems to predominantly activate microglia, exacerbating neuronal damage (Xie et al., 2023). Consequently, the inhibition or deficiency of cGAS in AD models reduces AD pathology, neuroinflammation, and cognitive impairment (Xie et al., 2023). In summary, it has been consistently revealed that the cGAS-STING pathway undergoes activation during both brain aging and injury, as well as in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Across various studies, the manipulation of this pathway through genetic knockout of associated genes or inhibition via chemical interventions has largely demonstrated a reduction in neuronal injury and an improvement in disease outcomes. These compelling results strongly indicate a primarily adverse impact of the cGAS–STING pathway in these conditions, underscoring its significance as a potential target for therapeutic interventions. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of understanding the potential contribution of each cell type in this context. cGAS–STING signaling in brain endothelial cells: Currently, the cell type-specific role of cGAS–STING signaling in the brain is poorly understood. The cGAS–STING pathway has been shown to be activated predominantly in microglia (Gulen et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023), but it is also present in astrocytes and neurons. While there is little research on the importance of cGAS–STING activity specifically in BECs in neurodegenerative diseases, its significance has been explored in the context of aging (Yu et al., 2022) and various diseases, such as diabetic retinopathy (Liu et al., 2023), COVID-19 (Domizio et al., 2022), and cerebral malaria (Pais et al., 2022). The common activators of the cGAS–STING pathway mentioned above, such as viral, bacterial, and self-DNA, have been shown to activate this pathway in BECs. During aging, mitochondrial dysfunction in blood vessels leads to the release of mtDNA into the cytoplasm. Simultaneously, nuclear DNA damage increases the amount of cytoplasmic chromatin fragments. These processes activate the cGAS–STING pathway in endothelial cells, contributing to aging-related endothelial dysfunction. Evidence of the activation of the cGAS-STING pathway is shown by the increased expression of cGAS, STING, and p-IRF3 in older aortic endothelial cells compared with younger ones, both in aged mice and humans (Yu et al., 2022). Consequently, inhibiting cGAS or STING in aging models improves endothelial function, reduces senescence, and decreases the levels of aging markers (Yu et al., 2022). Diabetic retinopathy is a common microvascular complication in diabetes mellitus, characterized by damage to the retinal blood vessels, which can lead to vision impairment or even blindness. cGAS-STING was found to be crucial to retinal endothelial cell senescence, inflammation, and the consequent capillary degeneration (Liu et al., 2023). Interestingly, by measuring free-floating DNA in the diabetic eyes, significantly higher levels of extracellular DNA are observed in diabetic patients compared with nondiabetic controls, suggesting a key role for increased free-floating extracellular DNA in the activation of the cGAS–STING pathway (Liu et al., 2023). In COVID-19, infection with SARS-CoV-2 causes mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA release in endothelial cells in the skin, lungs, and brain, which activates cGAS–STING signaling, leading to cell death and type I IFN production. This process is a key driver of the overall inflammatory response, significantly contributing to the pathogenesis of COVID-19 (Domizio et al., 2022). Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of STING reduces severe lung inflammation induced by SARS-CoV-2 and improves disease outcomes in mice. In further support of the role of BEC cGAS-STING signaling in brain disease, a recent study showed that BECs are the main cell drivers of the STING1-IFN axis in the brain during cerebral malaria, a fatal neurological complication of malaria infection (Pais et al., 2022). The study identified extracellular particles released from Plasmodium (the parasite responsible for malaria)-infected erythrocytes bind STING1 and activate the STING1-dependent type I IFN response in BECs (Pais et al., 2022). Furthermore, it pinpointed heme, a product of hemoglobin degradation within these extracellular particles, as a potential STING1 ligand. In addition, a recent study has shown that cGAS-STING signaling can also be activated in ECs independently of the DNA sensing pathway, for example, by vascular endothelial growth factor (Luo et al., 2023). Vascular endothelial growth factor activates the pathway by stimulating cGAS nuclear translocation via an importin-β pathway. Activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs results in increased production of type I IFNs and other cytokines (Figure 1). Type I IFNs from BECs, together with those from microglia, astrocytes, and neurons, elicit the interferon response, exacerbating or possibly even initiating neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. They signal through the heterodimeric receptor (IFNAR) and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling cascade, activating IFN signaling and stimulating the transcription of interferon-stimulated genes (Paul et al., 2021). These interferon-stimulated genes include proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. In addition to their role in natural immunity, interferon-stimulated genes are essential in the pathogenesis of CNS disorders including neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases (Paul et al., 2021). Type I IFNs produced by other cell types or by the endothelium itself can activate the IFNAR on BECs, i.e., binding to IFNARs on BECs in an autocrine and paracrine fashion. Activation of the IFN signaling pathway in BECs can result in neurovascular inflammation and BBB leakiness through multiple mechanisms: (1) Promoting endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, senescence, or death (Domizio et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023); (2) Impairing BBB integrity by downregulation of adherens junction protein VE-cadherin and tight junction proteins such as occludin and claudin-5 (Jana et al., 2022); (3) Enhancing leukocyte recruitment and infiltration (Pais et al., 2022). These findings prompt us to propose the significance of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Indeed, elevated STING expression is observed primarily in BECs in various neurodegenerative diseases including AD, PD, ALS, and multiple sclerosis (Ferecsko et al., 2023). Consistent with this, recent single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing of BECs from aged mice and human AD brains (Yang et al., 2022) has revealed heightened IFN inflammatory responses and IFN expression, hinting a possible role of the cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in the context of aging and AD. We therefore propose that the abnormal activation of the cGAS–STING pathway in BECs not only triggers BEC inflammation and dysfunction, but also exacerbates or even initiates a cascade of events culminating in the unrestrained and prolonged synthesis of inflammatory genes. Concurrently, the BBB’s integrity is compromised, marked by increased permeability and leakage. BBB disruption then facilitates the infiltration of harmful peripheral substances into the brain parenchyma, fueling the escalation of neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration (Figure 1). BBB dysfunction is a pathological hallmark shared by both aging and AD and is believed to play a pivotal role in driving downstream neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline (Sweeney et al., 2019). However, while appreciation of the pathological significance of BBB dysfunction has been growing, the direct cause-and-effect link between BBB dysfunction and disease progression, as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying BBB dysfunction, is still not fully understood. Activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs may offer a potential molecular mechanism in understanding this connection and BBB dysfunction. Conclusions and perspectives: Excessive cGAS–STING activity in microglia, astrocytes, and neurons occupy an important role in the inflammation and pathogenesis of brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases, but BECs also have high cGAS–STING activity under these conditions (Ferecsko et al., 2023). The significance of cGAS–STING activation in peripheral ECs across various diseases prompts us to contemplate the potential importance of cGAS–STING in BECs in the context of aging and neurodegeneration. We hypothesize that aberrant activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs may trigger neurovascular inflammation and play a pivotal role in aging and neurodegeneration. Therefore, targeting cGAS–STING activation in BECs may attenuate endothelial dysfunction and brain inflammation, and should be an intriguing avenue for future inquiry regarding brain aging and neurodegeneration. Targeting signaling pathways in BECs offers a potential advantage of bypassing the BBB, a significant challenge in drug development. To date, few studies have examined the role of the cGAS–STING pathway in BECs in neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, further research using BEC-specific approaches is needed to evaluate this hypothesis. BECs in arterial, capillary, and venous locations exhibit differences in transcriptomes in response to circulatory cues related to aging, innate immunity, and oxidative stress, with more significant changes in capillary BECs (Yang et al., 2022). It would be interesting to investigate whether the location of BECs exhibits differences in the activity and response of the cGAS–STING pathway during disease. As discussed above, cGAS–STING signaling can also be activated in ECs independently of the DNA sensing pathway (Luo et al., 2023). This raises an intriguing question: Can the cGAS–STING pathway be triggered in a DNA-independent manner in the context of neurodegeneration, and what roles do DNA-dependent and DNA-independent mechanisms play in this process? Another area of research is to study the interplay between BECs and the component cells of the brain. Could disruptions in the pathway within the brain cells produce secondary alterations in the endothelium? Answers to these questions will provide significant insights into this innate immune system and have therapeutic implications for treating neurodegenerative diseases.
